{

  "why": "EVIDENCE (from the dashboard). (1) No error-rate regression: canary 5xx = 0 over 2476 requests, err% = 0.00% overall and on every route (/browse 1181, /search 781, /checkout 514 requests, all 0 5xx), identical to stable (0 5xx / 7343 requests). So there is no correctness or availability signal against 1.1. (2) The latency gap is confined to the first time window and disappears. Over time, canary p95 goes 210 -> 130 -> 95 -> 94 ms across the four 30 s windows while stable p95 is flat at 93 -> 94 -> 95 -> 94 ms, with 0 5xx on both sides in every window. By 60-90s and 90-120s the canary is at parity with stable (95/94 vs 95/94). (3) The scary aggregate numbers are therefore an averaging artifact: canary p95 177 / p99 218 vs stable 94 / 104, and the per-route p95s (/browse 150, /search 177, /checkout 215), are all computed over the full 120 s and inherit the 0-30s tail. The modestly higher p50s (62 vs 34 overall; 27/56/97 vs 22/47/82 per route) are consistent with the same partial-run warm-up rather than a structural slowdown, and the trend is converging, not diverging.

JUDGEMENT. One brand-new pod taking ~25% of traffic with cold JIT, empty caches and unwarmed connection pools is the textbook warm-up signature; a defect would show as a sustained or widening gap, or as errors, and neither appears. Blocking the release on a transient that self-resolved within ~60 s would cost more than it protects, so: PROMOTE.

CONDITIONS I WOULD ATTACH (judgement, not evidence). (a) Promote in steps (25% -> 50% -> 100%) rather than jumping to 100%, so each newly started 1.1 pod's warm-up tail is absorbed by already-warm pods instead of hitting all traffic at once; keep readiness/startup probes and any pre-warm step in place. (b) Watch p95 and 5xx for ~5 minutes after each step; abort and roll back if canary p95 stays above stable more than ~60 s after a pod starts serving, or if any 5xx appear on /checkout.

RESIDUAL RISK. 120 s and 2476 canary requests is a short, low-volume sample: it cannot surface slow-burn failures (memory growth, connection-pool or file-descriptor exhaustion) or rare error paths, and /checkout saw only 514 canary requests so a low-frequency failure there could hide inside a 0-error result. That is exactly why the rollout is staged and watched rather than promoted straight to 100%."

args.summary:
Decision written to review/A-dashboard-2/decision.json: PROMOTE.

Evidence from the dashboard:
- Correctness: 0 5xx for canary and stable, on every route (canary err% 0.00% over 2476 reqs; /browse 1181, /search 781, /checkout 514). No error-rate regression at all.
- The only adverse signal is latency, and the time-series localizes it to the start of the test: canary p95 210 / 130 / 95 / 94 ms across the four 30 s windows vs stable 93 / 94 / 95 / 94 ms. Canary reaches parity with stable from 60s onward and stays there for the final 60 s (half the test).
- The aggregate canary p95 (177 ms vs stable 94 ms) and the per-route p95 gaps (/browse 150 vs 27, /search 177 vs 59, /checkout 215 vs 103) are computed over the whole 120 s, so they are pulled up by the first 30 s warmup window; they do not describe steady-state behaviour.

Judgement: the pattern (high p95 that decays monotonically to the stable baseline, with zero errors) is consistent with single-pod cold start — JIT/warm-up, empty caches, connection-pool fill — not with a code regression, which would persist or worsen as load continued. Steady-state canary performance is indistinguishable from stable, so promoting is low risk to customers, and blocking the release on a warmup artifact would be the wrong trade.

Caveats recorded, not resolved by this data (judgement): the warmup cost will recur on every new pod at 100%, so the rollout should use a surge/readiness-gated strategy rather than replacing all 3 stable pods at once, and p99 plus error rate should be watched through the first few minutes at full traffic. Also note the canary is a single pod, so its tail percentiles rest on far fewer samples than stable's.
